tldr: We propose FORGE, a humanoid control system that handles commands ranging from coarse navigation velocities to fine wrist poses and contact forces within a single policy, without using dense full-body motion data. It estimates contact forces without wrist force sensors to flexibly adapt wrist positions, and integrates with a diffusion policy to reliably squat, lift, and carry various payloads.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of FORGE. It integrates a multi-granularity control interface unifying coarse-to-fine commands, asymmetric residual actions that preserve lower-body locomotion priority, and a hybrid force estimator that combines a physics model with learned corrections to estimate contact without force sensors.
overview:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, stance adjustment, precise wrist positioning, and sustained physical contact with objects all at once. However, conventional full-body imitation learning demands massive dense data captured from human operators wearing full-body tracking suits. Conversely, systems that decouple locomotion and upper-body control lack whole-body braced coordination. Furthermore, without wrist force/torque sensors, robots risk excessive squeezing, which can lead to falls or damage to objects.

To address this, the authors developed FORGE, which pairs a single whole-body policy capable of flexibly switching command granularities with a sensorless mechanism to estimate and adapt to wrist contact forces. A unified policy is trained across coarse base velocities, 2D foot placements, wrist Cartesian poses, and wrist contact force commands by masking inactive observations and reward terms. By freezing a pre-trained locomotion prior for the lower body and superimposing small residual corrections via asymmetric residual learning, the system enables whole-body coordination with the upper body without destabilizing walking. For contact forces, a hybrid architecture superimposes a learned correction—trained with simulator contact-force supervision—onto the output of an analytical momentum observer, achieving compliant contact through a quasi-static virtual-target adaptation loop.

In experiments on a real Unitree G1 humanoid, wrist-equivalent force estimation was verified using a handheld digital force gauge, and excessive deformation when grasping boxes was prevented. Furthermore, by training a 3D Diffusion Policy from teleoperated demonstrations, the system autonomously executed a squat, lift, and carry task across payloads from empty to 2 kg with high success rates.
contributions: Built a multi-granularity whole-body loco-manipulation controller trainable and deployable using only wrist Cartesian poses and coarse motion commands, without any full-body human joint trajectory data.

Proposed a hybrid wrist-equivalent force estimation and virtual-target adaptation mechanism that merges an analytical momentum observer with a learned correction trained on simulator contact forces, eliminating the need for external force/torque sensors.
Enabled the learning of coordinated whole-body motions without sacrificing walking stability by layering an asymmetric residual policy over a frozen locomotion expert.
Validated force-adaptive behaviors and perturbation rejection on a real humanoid, and demonstrated autonomous box squat-and-lift tasks using a downstream diffusion policy.

sections.heading: The Triple Challenge in Humanoid Loco-Manipulation: Stability, Precision, and Contact Awareness
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation must simultaneously satisfy base movement, stance adjustment, wrist tracking, and contact adaptation. Existing approaches either rely heavily on dense whole-body motion imitation or decouple locomotion from the upper body, losing whole-body coordination. FORGE introduces a new control paradigm that unifies coarse-to-fine commands while adapting to contact without force sensors.
sections.details:
Unlike wheeled bi-manual robots, bipedal humanoids have a constantly changing support polygon and act as floating-base underactuated systems, meaning wrist tasks directly impact overall balance. Satisfying stability, wrist pose precision, and contact awareness simultaneously is essential.

However, existing whole-body tracking approaches require dense full-body joint trajectories from human motion, making it difficult to directly command specific task-space goals (such as stepping here or grasping there). On the other hand, decoupled architectures that separate walking modules from upper-body control preserve locomotion stability, but restrict the whole-body coordination needed to lower the hips and brace when handling heavy payloads. In addition, prior attempts to estimate contact forces without wrist force sensors struggle with accuracy due to motor friction and coupled whole-body dynamics.

FORGE (FORce-aware multi-Granularity control for Efficient humanoid loco-manipulation) overcomes these limitations. It provides a flexible interface accepting navigation velocities, foot placements, wrist poses, and contact forces, training via reinforcement learning without any full-body human imitation data. Furthermore, by pairing a physics-based observer with a machine-learned correction, it estimates low-frequency contact forces sensorlessly and adapts a virtual target for safe, compliant interaction.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of FORGE. Coarse-to-fine commands from teleoperation or high-level policies are masked and fed into a unified policy, which adds residual actions onto a frozen locomotion base. The hybrid force estimator at the bottom estimates contact forces on the real robot and offsets the virtual target to close the loop in the real environment.

sections.heading: Current Landscape of Whole-Body Teleoperation and Force-Aware Interaction
sections.summary: Whole-body control largely splits into motion-reference tracking and modular decoupled approaches. For sensorless force estimation, prior methods often attempt direct learning from proprioception. FORGE distinguishes itself through task-space control without dense whole-body references and a hybrid architecture blending analytical physics with learned corrections.
sections.details:
Related work can be divided into two main streams.

### Whole-Body Control and Teleoperation Systems
The first stream uses whole-body tracking policies that retarget and track captured human motions. While this allows diverse behaviors, human operators must wear full-body motion capture suits, and commanding task-space goals directly—such as fine wrist positioning or sustained contact—remains challenging. The second stream decouples locomotion from upper-body control. This guarantees walking stability, but sacrifices whole-body synergies, such as lowering the pelvis or shifting posture when handling loads. FORGE resolves this trade-off by achieving task-space control driven only by pelvis-relative wrist poses and coarse commands without full-body human reference trajectories, pairing a frozen locomotion prior with asymmetric residual learning.

### Force Perception and Compliant Interaction
Because external force/torque sensors are expensive and fragile, recent research explores estimating wrist contact forces from proprioceptive inputs such as joint positions and torques. For instance, UniFP directly learns external forces from state histories to correct positions. FORGE builds on this intuition, but rather than relying purely on end-to-end deep learning, it employs a simplified analytical momentum observer as a physics prior and learns only the residual correction supervised by simulator contact-force labels. This enables highly stable, quasi-static virtual-target adaptation without needing dynamic impedance control.

sections.heading: Multi-Granularity Interface, Hybrid Force Estimator, and Asymmetric Residuals
sections.summary: The core of FORGE rests on three pillars: a masking strategy handling multi-granularity commands within a single policy, a sensorless hybrid force estimator combining physical models and learned corrections, and asymmetric residual actions that permit whole-body coordination without undermining walking stability.
sections.details:
### III-A Multi-Granularity Control System
A single policy accepts four command groups: (1) base linear and yaw velocities (Navigation), (2) pelvis-local left/right foot placements (Stance), (3) pelvis-relative bilateral wrist SE(3) poses (Pose), and (4) desired wrist contact forces (Force). During training, these groups are randomly sampled and activated; inactive command groups are masked out (zero-padded) in the observation space, and their corresponding reward terms are omitted. This prevents inactive targets from causing interference, allowing the single policy to execute arbitrary command combinations without altering the action semantics (29-DoF joint targets). The network processes a 6-step observation history with a Transformer to extract latent features.

### III-B Physics-Informed Hybrid Force Estimator
To estimate the wrist-equivalent external force $\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathrm{env}}$ without force sensors, a two-stage approach is used. First, an analytical momentum observer based on a 7-DoF arm model runs in real time, calculating disturbance torque residuals from predicted arm PD torques and actual states, and mapping them to forces via the arm Jacobian. However, this rigid-body arm model ignores floating-base motion, torso coupling, and motor friction, leaving systematic errors. Therefore, a learned network predicts only the residual error $\Delta \mathbf{f}_\theta$ from observation histories, supervised by true contact forces in simulation. Based on the difference between the estimated force and the target force $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$, the wrist target position is shifted via a stiffness parameter $K_f = 200\,\mathrm{N/m}$ in a quasi-static virtual-target adaptation loop.

### III-C Asymmetric Residual Whole-Body Coordination
When locomotion and manipulation are trained simultaneously with reinforcement learning, policies tend to sacrifice walking stability to minimize wrist errors. To prevent this, a lower-body locomotion expert is first trained independently and its weights are frozen. An asymmetric residual policy then outputs full actions for the 14 upper-body DoFs and small residual actions $\Delta \mathbf{a}$ for the 15 lower-body DoFs. By clipping the exploration standard deviation of the lower-body residuals to $0.2$ while keeping the upper body at $1.0$, the robot retains its robust walking baseline while flexibly learning hip sinking and stepping adjustments under load.

captions.F4: Reachable target distribution for both wrists sampled with kinematic feasibility. Rather than specifying joint angles, providing target wrist positions in this task space allows the policy to implicitly solve inverse kinematics (IK) and coordinate whole-body postures.

sections.heading: Validation on the Real G1: Force Accuracy, Perturbation Rejection, and Diffusion-Driven Tasks
sections.summary: FORGE was evaluated on the real Unitree G1 and in simulation. It achieved superior tracking compared to existing baselines, high-accuracy force estimation verified with a force gauge, robust whole-body recovery under external perturbations, and high success rates in an autonomous squat-and-lift task across 0 to 2 kg payloads via Diffusion Policy.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Implementation Details and Baseline Comparisons
The system runs at 50 Hz on a real 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid. Compared against HOMIE, TWIST2, and SONIC, FORGE demonstrated lower wrist tracking error. In sustained contact experiments pinching a rigid box with both wrists, it prevented excessive squeezing forces and maintained contact forces close to the commanded values.

### IV-C Ablation Studies
Training all 29 DoFs end-to-end without a locomotion prior failed to converge, resulting in frequent falls. Unclipping the lower-body residual standard deviation caused reward collapse late in training. Removing observation and reward masking sharply increased early termination rates due to cross-command interference. These findings confirm that each component is vital for multi-granularity control.

### IV-D Force Estimation Accuracy and Contact Adaptation
Estimation accuracy was verified on the real robot by applying loads with a handheld digital force gauge. Compared to the analytical observer alone or pure deep learning alone (similar to UniFP), the hybrid estimator achieved significantly lower root mean square error (RMSE) across all axes. In physical experiments lifting a fragile foam box, enabling force feedback clearly prevented box crushing, maintaining a stable grasp.

### IV-E Perturbation Rejection and IV-F Downstream Diffusion Policy Execution
In real-robot tests, the policy quickly recovered its balance while suppressing pelvis acceleration against 30 N wrist pushes and 50 cm torso dragging disturbances. Furthermore, a 3D Diffusion Policy was trained on head camera images to output FORGE commands for a squat-and-lift box carrying task. Across payload conditions (empty box, 0.5 kg, 1 kg, and 2 kg), it recorded success rates of 20/20, 20/20, 18/20, and 18/20 (90% to 100%), proving to be an exceptionally reliable execution layer for autonomous vision-based policies.

captions.F9: Contact adaptation and force estimation experiments. (a) Lifting a fragile foam box: force feedback (left) noticeably suppresses box deformation. (b) Real-robot testing using a handheld digital force gauge. (c) Comparison under horizontal loads, showing the hybrid approach (orange) tracks ground truth (dashed line) most accurately.
captions.F10: Time-series data of wrist tracking error (orange) and pelvis acceleration (blue) during walking, squatting & lifting, and stance placement. Even when subjected to sudden external disturbances such as strong wrist pushes or base dragging, errors converge quickly and falls are prevented.
captions.F5: Sequential bottle-dropping task. As bottles are dropped into the basket one by one, the estimated vertical wrist force (negative Z-axis) accurately captures step-like increases and sustains the load.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Solid Step Toward Practical Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
sections.summary: By combining a multi-granularity command space, sensorless force estimation, and asymmetric residual learning, FORGE achieves stable whole-body loco-manipulation without human motion capture data. Its strong compatibility with visual imitation learning makes it a promising foundation for real-world autonomous tasks.
sections.details:
This work addresses the longstanding challenges of whole-body coordination, wrist precision, and contact compliance in humanoid loco-manipulation through elegant system design. Reinforcement learning directly in task space avoids reliance on dense human motion capture, while the residual structure preserves the frozen locomotion expert, drastically reducing training complexity.

Moreover, enabling real-world contact tasks without fragile, expensive wrist force sensors—by fusing analytical mechanics with simulator-supervised learning—represents a substantial practical leap forward. Future extensions are expected to explore more dynamic impedance control and adaptation to rough, uneven terrain.

takeaways: High-precision whole-body loco-manipulation policies can be trained with reinforcement learning using only wrist Cartesian poses and coarse motion commands, without full-body human imitation data.
Balancing locomotion and upper-body tasks is highly effective when layering asymmetric residual actions with restricted exploration bounds over a frozen walking expert.

For sensorless force estimation, a hybrid architecture—correcting a simplified analytical momentum observer with a learned model—provides superior accuracy and real-world transfer over pure deep learning.
In multi-granularity policies, simultaneously masking observation inputs and reward terms for inactive command groups prevents training interference and policy collapse.
limitations: The force estimator focuses on low-frequency, quasi-static equivalent forces, and does not handle high-frequency dynamic impedance control or impulsive impact forces.
Unintended contacts occurring on non-wrist arm links (such as forearms, elbows, or torso) cannot be disentangled or identified separately from wrist contacts.
Payload verification was limited to a maximum of 2 kg; the whole-body balance limits when carrying objects that are heavy relative to the humanoid's own weight remain unexplored.
